panels.rationale: Whole-figure plate of 3 panels (a, b, c). a: The caption identifies a real 13-year-old patient subsequently diagnosed with Gaucher disease and describes radiographic periosteal reaction and intramedullary sclerosis in the distal femur. [raw subtype: non-neuronopathic] b: The caption specifically attributes the MRI abnormalities in this patient to intramedullary marrow edema and focal subperiosteal fluid thought to represent subperiosteal hemorrhage in Gaucher disease. [raw subtype: non-neuronopathic] c: The MRI directly demonstrates serpiginous peripheral enhancement of distal femoral bone infarcts, explicitly attributed in the caption to this patient with Gaucher disease. [raw subtype: non-neuronopathic]

panels.figure_caption: Bone infarct and subperiosteal hemorrhage mimicking osteomyelitis in Gaucher disease. A 13-year-old male presented with atraumatic knee pain and swelling. Initial lateral knee radiograph (a) showed subtle periosteal reaction along the posterior metadiaphysis of the distal femur and ill-defined intramedullary sclerosis within the femoral shaft. Follow-up MRI demonstrated intramedullary marrow edema and focal subperiosteal fluid with surrounding inflammatory changes in the popliteal fossa thought to be related to subperiosteal hemorrhage on axial T2-weighted image (b). Coronal post-contrast T1 fat-saturated image (c) demonstrated peripheral serpentine enhancement of areas of bone infarction within the distal femur. The patient was subsequently diagnosed with Gaucher disease after initial workup for hematopoietic malignancy

Likewise, the microscopy report of the specimen revealed autolytic and ischemic changes along with the marked expansion of the red pulp with a large number of histiocytic cells with finely fibrillary cytoplasm, particularly in the splenic cords. The white pulp was intact and preserved (Fig. 2). Then differential diagnosis was discussed again with the multidisciplinary team, and the team of pathologists decided it was consistent with Gaucher’s disease, type 1, with ischemic changes. Postoperatively, recovery was uneventful, and there were no complications during follow-up at 2 and 4 weeks.
